RRPs in Europe: from representation to power 📈

Why are we not seeing widespread countermobilization against radical right success?

Preview ⏩️

  • Question: Why are we not seeing widespread countermobilization against radical right success?
  • Argument: drawing on intergroup threat theory
    • symbolically threatened groups not concerned
    • realistically threatened groups show pragmatic electoral responses and protest mobilization
  • Empirical Strategy:
    • Descriptive: open-ended most-important-problem responses
    • Electoral Effects: Staggered DiD around concern-onset
  • Results:
    • preliminary analysis confirms pragmatic electoral responseaimed to curb RRP success

Theory

  • Intergroup Threat Theory (Stephan, Ybarra, and Morrison 2009):
    • symbolic threat: to values, beliefs, identity
    • realistic threat to resources, power, physical wellbeing
    • subjective perceptions matter, not objective conditions

\(\rightarrow\) Symbolic threat triggers distinction, realistic threat triggers pragmatic responses

Argument:

  • symbolic threat of RRP governance is universal
  • realistic threat is unequally distributed

Who faces realistic threat?

  • migrant (background) communities
    • key out-group within radical right politics
    • to face policy and everyday discrimination, exclusion and potentially violence
  • young women
    • sexism and anti-feminist backlash important dimensions of RRP success
    • young women navigate (higher) education, labor market integration, and …
    • family formation, which concerns sexual self-determination and reproductive rights

Expected Pragmatic Responses

  • Strategic voting
    • support for established parliamentary parties to ensure impact in seat allocation
    • strategic compromise in tight SMD races
  • Overshooting to the left
    • perception of right-tilt leads to overcompensation to the left, even if not fully aligned with preferences
    • across the ideological spectrum
  • Protest mobilization
    • non-electoral mobilization to signal opposition and empower ingroup

Empirical Strategy

  • Case & data:
    • German Longitudinal Election Study (GLES), since 2017
    • open-ended most-important problem (MIP) responses
  • Descriptive analysis:
    • Who flags RRP success as a problem?
  • Causal analysis of downstream electoral effects:
    • Staggered DiD around concern-onset
    • Party choice, party favorability + placebo outcomes

Next Steps

  • incorporate LGBTQIA+ community into theory? what about homonationalism?
  • migrant (background) communities underrepresented in the current data
  • extend outcome scope to all theoretically relevant behaviors, particularly protest mobilization

Conclusion & Contribution

  • Reactions to RRP success are shaped by threat perceptions, which are unequally distributed
  • Concerned voters show pragmatic electoral responses
    • support for parliamentary parties, overshooting to the left

Contribution:

  • extends supporter-focused RRP research (Valentim 2024, 2021)
  • beyond entry into parliament as point of observation (Bischof and Wagner 2019; Castanho Silva 2018)
  • speaks to broader debates on role of sexism and gender gaps within RRP politics (Milosav et al. 2025; Anduiza and Rico 2024)
